chapter.title: Six Ways to Make People Like You
chapter.hook: The fastest way to be remembered kindly is to spend the first minute asking about the photograph on the dresser, not the person in the bed.
chapter.counterintuition: Most readers assume being likable is about what you bring to a room, your warmth, your wit, your good listening face. It is almost entirely about what you withhold, which is talk about yourself, long enough for the other person to feel like the more interesting one.
chapter.keyTakeaway: Spend your attention on what the other person already cares about; ask about the one specific thing on their desk or in their story, then close your mouth and listen.

breakdown.fastRead:
A man in hospice had quit talking to almost everyone. A nurse named Ruth walked in and did not ask how he felt. She looked at the photograph on his dresser and said, 'That river. Tell me about that river.' He talked for twenty minutes, and a son who had not heard his father's voice in a week stood in the hallway and cried.

That is the whole of it, and it is not a trick. People warm to you when you are warm to them first, and warmth is honest interest in what they already care about. Not a script. Not flattery. The picture they framed. The dog asleep on their foot. The town they grew up in.

Ask about the one thing on their desk they already love, and then listen like you want the answer. Most people go a whole week without being asked a single question worth answering. Be the one who asks it.
breakdown.deepRead:
A high school basketball coach in Akron had a transfer player who would not look up during drills. By Friday the boy was ready to quit and tell his friends the program was cold. The coach pulled him aside and asked about his old gym. Just that. What was the floor like. Who ran the drills. What did the warm-up sound like. Three minutes of listening without correcting a thing. Only then did the coach mention tomorrow's plan, and the boy nodded.

This is what people mean when they call someone good with people. It is not charm. Early in the conversation, you decide to spend your attention on the other person's life instead of broadcasting your own. You take what they care about seriously enough to ask about it.

The move has two parts. First, find the one specific thing on their desk, on their wall, on their hoodie that they already love. A framed river. An old gym. A band logo. Second, ask about that one thing in particular, not about life in general, and then close your mouth.

Watch what happens at a hotel front desk at two in the morning when a stranded traveler is furious. The night auditor does not defend the hotel. She asks his name. She uses it. She asks where he was supposed to be tonight. He was supposed to be at his daughter's recital, six hours away, and he had already missed it. The anger goes out of him before she has typed a word, because someone finally treated him like a man with somewhere he had been trying to be.

Curiosity you do not feel is theater, and the other person can feel it across a counter. Ask the question whose answer you actually want to hear.
breakdown.fullRead:
A small-practice tax preparer in Cleveland was thirty minutes behind on the worst day of his April. A widow sat across from him and kept apologizing for asking the same question twice. He could have moved her along. Instead, when she mentioned her late husband's first name, he repeated it back gently, and twenty minutes later he used it again, as if he had known the man. She came back the next year, when her return was genuinely complicated, and she brought her sister. He spent twenty extra minutes that day and earned two clients for life.

This is the older question. Not the persuasion of an argument, not the closing of a sale, but whether someone wants to be in a room with you at all. Liking comes before reasoning. If a person does not feel welcome around you, nothing clever you say next is going to land.

Spend your attention on what makes the other person feel important before you say one thing about yourself. Their name. The photograph on their desk. The job they did before this one. The book they picked up first at the fair. None of these are tricks. They are the ordinary furniture of another person's life, and most adults walk through their week with no one noticing any of it.

A dental hygienist tried weather and weekend plans on a sixteen-year-old in earbuds and got nothing back. Then she noticed the band logo on his hoodie and asked one specific question about the drummer. He pulled out an earbud to answer. That was the whole opening. Not because she was a fan. Because she looked at him long enough to find a real thing to ask about.

Notice what is missing in all of these. No one is performing warmth. No one is running a script. Ruth, the hospice nurse, is not running a maneuver called Compliment The Patient's Belongings. She is interested. The coach in Akron wants to know about the old gym. The auditor at two in the morning is not soothing the guest, she is finding out where he was trying to spend his night. People can feel the difference between someone curious about them and someone curious about closing them, and the second one always shows.

The performed version collapses inside a sentence. The eyes drift. The follow-up question never lands on the answer you just gave, it lands on the next item on your list. Anyone who has sat through a working-the-room conversation knows that feeling, and it is the opposite of welcome. I have been on both ends of it, and I am not proud of either.

There is one more piece you can carry. When you give the other person room to talk about their own life, you give yourself an easier job than the one you came in with. You no longer have to be impressive. You only have to be attentive. A line cook in Pittsburgh, newly promoted to expediter, learned the name of every server who came to the pass, and on the busiest Saturday of the month he called each one by name as their plates left the window. Less food came back. Not because the cooking changed. Because the mood did, and the mood changed because one man bothered to notice.

Find one true thing about the person in front of you, and say it before you ask for anything at all.

examples.title: Fenella's First Visit With the Man Who Won't Speak

planSpec.domain: a hospice nurse arriving for her first visit with a man who has stopped speaking to most visitors
planSpec.audience: a hospice nurse three months into her first hospice rotation
planSpec.stakes: whether she gets the patient to say a single full sentence today, which his daughter has begged for
planSpec.requiredBeat: she opens by asking about the framed photograph on his dresser, not about how he is feeling, and he begins to talk about the river in the picture

examples.scenario: Fenella sets her bag down in the doorway of room 12 on a Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Eberhardt is turned toward the window, jaw set, the way his daughter warned her he would be. On the dresser sits a framed photograph: a younger him in waders, knee-deep in a wide brown river, holding up a small fish. She has the standard opening on her tongue, how are you feeling today, and she can already hear the silence that will follow it. Her eyes go back to the photograph. She is about to choose between the script and the river.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the health question. Walk to the dresser, point at the photograph, and ask what river that is and what he caught that day.
examples.whyItMatters: A sick man has been asked about his body all week by strangers. The photograph is the one thing in the room that says he was once somebody, and asking about it lets him answer as that man.

examples.title: Coach Quill Asks Devontae About His Old Gym

planSpec.domain: a high school basketball coach trying to reach a transfer player who will not make eye contact at practice
planSpec.audience: a coach in the second week of a new season
planSpec.stakes: whether the player stays on the roster or quits by Friday and tells his friends the program is cold
planSpec.requiredBeat: the coach asks about the player's old gym, listens for three full minutes without correcting anything, and only then mentions tomorrow's drill

examples.scenario:
Devontae is shooting free throws alone at the far hoop, hood up, eyes on the floor. Coach Quill walks over, leans on the stanchion, and waits until the next miss.

"That gym you came from. Hartwell, right? I heard their court has a dead spot near the visitor bench."

Devontae glances up. "Two of them. One under the logo. Coach D taped a quarter to the floor so we'd remember."

"Tell me about Coach D."

Devontae starts talking. Quill says nothing for a long time.
examples.whatToDo: Ask one specific question about his old gym, then keep your mouth shut for three full minutes. Only after he stops talking, mention tomorrow's drill.
examples.whyItMatters: A player who has not been heard cannot hear you. His attention is locked on defending himself until someone proves the room is safe, and questions about his past prove it faster than promises about the future.

examples.title: Magnus and the Widow Who Keeps Apologizing

planSpec.domain: a tax preparer sitting with a recently widowed woman who keeps apologizing for asking the same question twice
planSpec.audience: a small-practice tax preparer who is already running thirty minutes late on the day
planSpec.stakes: whether the client trusts him enough to come back next April, when her return becomes genuinely complicated
planSpec.requiredBeat: he repeats her late husband's first name back to her gently when she mentions it, and uses that same name again twenty minutes later as if he had known the man

examples.scenario: It is 4:10 on a Tuesday in March and Magnus, a tax preparer who runs his practice out of a converted dentist's office, is thirty minutes behind. Across the desk sits Mrs. Halloway, holding a manila envelope with both hands. She has just asked him a second time how the standard deduction works, and apologized for it. "I'm sorry, my husband Reuben always did these. I'm hopeless without him." Magnus sets down his pen. "Reuben handled them every year?" he says, softly, the name carried back to her the way she said it. Twenty minutes later, sliding the signature page across, he says, "Reuben would have wanted this filed clean. We're filing it clean." Her shoulders drop an inch.
examples.whatToDo: Catch the husband's name the first time it is spoken, repeat it back gently in her own cadence, and bring that same name back unprompted later in the visit.
examples.whyItMatters: A widow's grief is not a topic to manage; it is the room itself. Saying Reuben aloud tells her you saw the man, not just the return, and the trust that buys lasts longer than any tax tip.

examples.title: Tariq Calls Every Server by Name on a Saturday Rush

planSpec.domain: a head line cook newly promoted to expediter who decides to learn the name of every server who comes to the pass
planSpec.audience: a line cook in his first month running tickets
planSpec.stakes: whether the front of house begins to trust the kitchen instead of grumbling at it through the next Saturday rush
planSpec.requiredBeat: on the busiest service of the month he calls each server by name as their plates leave the window, and the floor returns less food, not because cooking changed but because mood did

examples.scenario: Before: Tariq's first three Saturdays as expediter, plates left the window without a word, and servers slid past the pass with their shoulders up, complaining at the bar that the kitchen ran cold. After: on the fourth Saturday, the busiest service of the month, he called each server by name as their plates left the window. Marguerite, table 14. Sun-Hee, table 6. Devon, your two-tops. By eleven the floor was sending less food back. Nothing in the cooking had changed. The mood had.
examples.whatToDo: Learn the name of every server who comes to your pass, then use it out loud the next time their food is up. Do it before they need a single thing from you.
examples.whyItMatters: A name said correctly tells someone they are a person to you, not a function. Servers who feel seen carry less resentment to the table, and the guest tastes the difference before the food does.

examples.title: Ophelia spots the band logo on a teenager's hoodie

planSpec.domain: a dental hygienist treating a sixteen-year-old who has shown up in earbuds and refuses small talk
planSpec.audience: a hygienist who has already tried weather and weekend plans and gotten nothing back
planSpec.stakes: whether the teenager will actually start flossing instead of lying about flossing for another six months
planSpec.requiredBeat: she notices the band logo on his hoodie and asks one specific question about the drummer in that band, and he pulls out an earbud to answer

examples.scenario: Ophelia is six minutes into cleaning a sixteen-year-old's molars when she gives up on weather and weekend plans. He has answered every question with a grunt through his earbuds. Then she sees the faded logo on his hoodie, a band she only knows because her nephew plays them too loud. She knows the drummer just left for a side project. Her gloved hand hovers near the suction wand. She can keep working in silence and hand him the same flossing speech he has nodded through twice a year since he was eleven, or she can pull back, ask him one specific question about that drummer, and wait.
examples.whatToDo: Ask one narrow question about the drummer who left the band, then stop talking. Let the earbud come out on his terms before you raise flossing.
examples.whyItMatters: A teenager who feels treated like a chart number lies about flossing. A teenager who feels seen as the person wearing that hoodie has a reason to come back honest.

examples.title: Yelena reconstructs the 2 a.m. complaint that almost broke her

planSpec.domain: a hotel night auditor on the front desk at 2 a.m. when a stranded business traveler walks in furious about a missed shuttle
planSpec.audience: a night auditor who has been told by her manager that she is too quiet to handle complaints
planSpec.stakes: whether the guest writes a one-star review or asks for her by name on his next trip through the city
planSpec.requiredBeat: she does not defend the hotel; she asks his name, uses it twice, and asks where he was supposed to be tonight, and the anger drains out of him before she has typed anything

examples.scenario: At shift change Yelena writes up the night for her manager, who has told her twice she is too quiet to work the desk. The traveler had walked in at 2:04 a.m., suitcase wheels barking on the tile, shouting that the shuttle had left him at the airport. She remembers the exact order. She did not defend the hotel. She asked his name. Hassan. She said it back, then asked where he had been trying to get to tonight. A wedding rehearsal in Newark, his sister's. By the second time she said Hassan, his shoulders had come down, and she had not yet touched the keyboard.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the script about policy. Ask the angry person's name, repeat it back, then ask where they were supposed to be tonight before you type a single thing into the system.
examples.whyItMatters: Anger at a counter is almost never about the counter. It is the feeling of being a case number in someone else's bad night. A name said twice converts a complainant back into a person, and people do not yell at someone who has already seen them.

examples.title: Hester at the book fair finds the right question for Eli

planSpec.domain: a parent volunteering at a fourth-grade book fair who notices a boy nobody is standing near
planSpec.audience: a parent who has always felt awkward around children who are not her own
planSpec.stakes: whether one quiet afternoon becomes a small lift this boy will remember the next time he feels invisible
planSpec.requiredBeat: she does not ask his grade or his favorite subject; she asks which book he picked up first and why, and he tells her at length while she does not interrupt once

examples.scenario: Hester is restocking the picture-book table when she notices a boy near the back, alone, holding a paperback like it might bite. Her usual instinct kicks in: ask his grade, ask his favorite subject, do the parent thing. She catches herself. Those are questions about him. He needs a question about the book. She kneels and asks Eli which one he picked up first, and why. He starts talking about a kid who builds a raft. He talks for four minutes. She does not interrupt once.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the demographic small talk. Ask which thing in front of him he reached for first, and why. Then close your mouth and let him finish his sentence twice over before you respond.
examples.whyItMatters: A child standing alone is starved for the experience of being interesting to someone. A question about the object he chose treats his taste as worth hearing. Grade and subject only file him into a category.

questions.prompt: Which of these best matches the rule for opening a conversation with someone you want to like you?
choices: Open with a fact about yourself that might impress them
Open with a specific question about something they already care about
Open with a polite, generic question about their weekend
questions.explanation: Specific questions about what someone already cares about make them feel attended to. Generic weekend questions feel like filler that nobody bothers answering, and self-promotion makes you the subject when the other person should be.

questions.prompt: A new account manager wonders why asking customers about their hobbies seems to soften tense calls before any business is discussed. What best explains the effect?
choices: Customers feel their attention has been taken seriously, which lowers defenses faster than reassurance does
Hobby talk burns clock time so the original complaint cools down on its own
It signals the company values work-life balance, which improves brand impression
questions.explanation: Real attention to a person's life lowers their guard far faster than any reassurance script. The other choices treat the effect as accidental or branding, missing that the warmth itself is doing the work.

questions.prompt: A children's librarian sees a nine-year-old standing alone near the graphic novels, ignored by his classmates on a field trip. She wants him to feel seen without making a scene. What is the soundest first move?
choices: Walk over, kneel down, and ask which book on the shelf he picked up first and why
Announce loudly that this corner has the best books so other kids drift over
Ask him how school is going and whether he likes reading in general
questions.explanation: Specific interest in what he is already holding signals real attention. Drawing other kids over makes him a public exhibit, which is the opposite of being seen. A generic school question is the kind nobody bothers answering honestly.

questions.prompt: A real estate agent meets a couple who lost a bidding war last weekend and now seem closed off on the second showing of a different house. What should she do before talking about this house?
choices: Highlight three features of this house that the previous one lacked
Reassure them the market is cooling and prices will likely fall
Ask what they liked most about the house they lost and listen until they finish
questions.explanation: What they lost is what they care about right now, so asking about it gives them the floor. Listing features pushes the agent's agenda before learning theirs. Market predictions sound like sales talk and do not earn trust at this moment.

questions.prompt: A vet tech notices a teenage owner staring at the floor while her old terrier is being weighed. The owner has barely spoken since arriving. What is the strongest opening?
choices: Reassure her that the terrier looks healthy for his age
Explain the next steps of the visit clearly so she knows what to expect
Ask the dog's name, use it twice, and ask how they first met
questions.explanation: Using the dog's name and asking how they met treats the bond as the thing that matters to her. Reassurance and procedural explanation skip past the owner to the chart, which is what most clinics already do.

questions.prompt: A newly hired director wants her team of eight engineers to actually trust her by the end of her first week. What single practice will move that fastest?
choices: Send a one-page memo describing her background and management philosophy
Sit one-on-one with each engineer and ask about a current project they care about, then listen
Hold a kickoff lunch and share three goals for the quarter
questions.explanation: Listening to each engineer talk about work they already care about builds more trust in a week than any memo or kickoff. The other choices keep the new boss as the subject of every interaction, which is exactly the wrong center of gravity.

questions.prompt: A sales rep keeps losing renewal calls. He opens each one by recapping his company's recent product wins, asks if there are questions, and then runs through pricing. Where is his approach going wrong?
choices: His pricing is being delivered too late in the call to register
He needs more product wins to recap, since the current list sounds thin
He is broadcasting his side before learning anything about what the customer is wrestling with
questions.explanation: He never asks the customer what they are actually working on, so renewals feel like a pitch aimed past them. Pricing timing and a longer recap are surface fixes that double down on the same self-centered opening.

questions.prompt: Two managers reply to the same frustrated customer email. Both apologize first. Manager A then explains the company's policy in detail. Manager B asks the customer what he had been trying to accomplish when the problem hit. Why does B's reply usually defuse the situation better?
choices: It shifts attention to the customer's own situation, which is the acknowledgment he was actually after
It avoids any mention of policy, which customers find legally threatening
It is shorter, and shorter replies always read as more sincere
questions.explanation: Asking about the customer's situation hands the floor back to him, which is the acknowledgment he was hoping for under the complaint. Avoiding policy or trimming length are mechanical fixes that miss the human one.

questions.prompt: A networking-event regular complains he meets dozens of people each month and never hears from any of them again. He hands out cards, mentions his title, and tells a story about his last big project. What is most likely missing from his approach?
choices: He is not following up by email within 24 hours of meeting them
His story about the big project needs to be tightened to under a minute
He is not asking each person about something they already care about and listening to the answer
questions.explanation: Cards, titles, and project stories all keep him at the center of every conversation, so people remember being talked at. Email follow-up and tighter stories do not fix the absence of curiosity that made him forgettable in the first place.

questions.prompt: At a parent-teacher conference, two teachers handle the same shy father differently. Teacher X opens with a list of his daughter's grades and behavior notes. Teacher Y asks what his daughter is like at home around her younger brother, and listens for two minutes. Which judgment is soundest?
choices: Teacher Y is wasting conference time that should be used for academic data
Teacher Y has earned more honest engagement for the harder feedback that follows
Teacher X is more professional because the agenda is the grades, not family life
questions.explanation: Asking about home life puts the father in the room as a person before the harder grade conversation arrives. Treating that as wasted time misses that honest engagement is what makes any feedback that follows actually land.

reviewCards.front: You sit down with someone you want to reach. Before you say anything about yourself or your agenda, what is the one move this calls for?
reviewCards.back: Spend your attention on what makes them feel important first. Find one specific thing on their desk, their wall, or their clothing that they already care about, ask about that one thing, and then close your mouth and listen.

reviewCards.front: A furious guest walks up to your counter at 2 a.m. ready to write a one-star review. Your instinct is to defend your company. What should you do instead?
reviewCards.back: Ask his name and use it. Ask where he was trying to be tonight. Treat him like a person with a life you do not yet know about, not a complaint to be processed. The anger usually drains before you have typed a word, because he feels seen.

reviewCards.front: A teenager in earbuds will not answer questions about weather, school, or weekend plans. What kind of question actually has a chance of working?
reviewCards.back: Skip the general categories and look for one specific signal already on him, like a band logo on a hoodie. Ask one narrow question about that thing, such as something about the drummer in that band. Specific curiosity gets an earbud pulled out; small talk does not.

reviewCards.front: A grieving client mentions her late husband's first name once, in passing. You are running thirty minutes late. What is the small move that earns her trust for next year?
reviewCards.back: Repeat his name back to her gently when she says it, and use that same name again later in the meeting as if you had known the man. Treating his name as worth holding onto tells her the person she lost still counts in the room, which is what she came in needing.

reviewCards.front: You catch yourself rehearsing what you will say next while the other person is still talking. What does this tell you, and what should you correct?
reviewCards.back: It tells you your curiosity has gone theatrical, and people feel that across a counter. Stop preparing your line and ask the question whose answer you actually want to hear, then let them finish. Attention you are faking is worse than no attention; attention you mean is the whole skill.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Specific curiosity. You learn to scan for the one concrete thing a person already cares about, a photograph, a hoodie, a hometown, and ask one real question about it before you say anything about yourself. Practiced enough, this stops feeling like a technique and starts feeling like the natural opening move of any conversation.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to start a one-on-one and you can already feel yourself rehearsing what you want to say, then look around their desk or screen for one specific object and open with a question about that instead.
If a family member mentions a person by name (a coworker, a friend, a doctor), then write that name down and use it correctly the next time they bring that person up, without prompting.
If a patient or client shows up guarded or rushing through answers, then find one detail they are wearing or carrying and ask one honest question about it before you reach for the form.
If you catch yourself answering a stranger's question with a story about yourself, then stop after one sentence and ask them the same question back, and actually wait for the answer.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, pick one person you see often but barely talk to, a barista, a coworker two desks over, your kid's bus driver, and ask them one specific question about something visible on them or near them. Listen for a full minute without steering the answer toward yourself.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a day this week, before any meeting or visit that matters, write down one thing you already know the other person cares about and one question you actually want the answer to. At the end of the week, look back at the seven questions and notice which ones opened the person up and which ones were polite filler.
